Tech Report: Strengthening the fight against online child sexual abuse with new tools and support

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.
  • According to recent reports, today, we’re releasing a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators.
  • According to recent reports, it is well⁠(opens in a latest window) established⁠(opens in a new window) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.

According to recent reports, today, we’re releasing a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators. These efforts build on our Child Safety Blueprint and our ongoing work to detect, block, and report abuse. For parents, the goal is simple: technology that helps keep children safe, with people in control.

According to recent reports, it is well⁠(opens in a latest window) established⁠(opens in a new window) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations. Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online.

Recent findings suggest that we’re building on our current protections with the release of a fresh image classifier that can detect potential CSAM, including AI-generated material. This new classifier looks for visual signs of abuse, helping teams identify novel images that may not have been seen before. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. This is the first CSAM classifier with broad availability that has a specific signal on indicating if CSAM may be AI generated.

Our teams trained, evaluated, and designed the classifier for real-world deployment with assistance from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)⁠(opens in a upcoming window), a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline, a centralized reporting hub for the online exploitation of children.

We’re offering access to the classifier to vetted organizations through the OpenAI API at no cost, making CSAM detection more accessible to child safety organizations and the broader industry, including those with teams of varying sizes.

Industry observers note that child safety is an industry-wide problem that requires strong collaboration across organizations and a variety of solutions. We’ve engaged the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window) and ROOST⁠(opens in a new window) to help us share access to this new tool, and we are strong supporters of tools developed by others such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window) CSAM detection system. In addition, we recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program⁠(opens in a new window), where we will share and receive signals relating to online child sexual exploitation and abuse to strengthen cross- platform collaboration.

Sources indicate that we’ve tested the classifier internally and with early partners to measure how much abusive material it detects, how often it flags other images, and how it can support safety teams. Their feedback helped us identify weaknesses and improve the system.

According to recent reports, early tests suggest the classifier can help reviewers focus on abusive images while reducing review of false positives. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, we compared the new classifier with our current protections and found:.

The new classifier could reduce review work: we estimated that it would flag 48% fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool.

Images flagged by the upcoming classifier were about twice as likely to contain abuse.

It has been revealed that early access partners have also evaluated how the classifier supports their own safety teams. In fal⁠(opens in a latest window)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed 72% of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM. invideo AI⁠(opens in a new window)’s testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban. In SafetyKit⁠(opens in a new window)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected 90% of cases.

More information about the classifier is available in the CSAM classifier model card⁠(opens in a latest window). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through our intake form⁠. We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

In a recent development, we already prohibit CSAM, train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with latest product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.

In a recent development, the warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.

We developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, including Protect Children⁠(opens in a fresh window), the Lucy Faithfull Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial⁠(opens in a new window) of deterrent messages.

The protection of children online doesn’t end with detection. We’ve published CSAM guidance⁠(opens in a upcoming window) to give developers practical steps to prevent abuse, detect harmful content, and act on it. Developed with input from the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), NCMEC⁠(opens in a new window), and the Internet Watch Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), it is designed for organizations at different stages of building their safety systems.

The guidance provides clear rules, ways for people to report concerns, detection tools, and processes for reviewing and reporting suspected abuse. It also explains how safety identifiers can help developers connect misuse to individual users and how to support the people reviewing sensitive content. Developers can use it alongside tools such as our latest image classifier, Moderation API⁠(opens in a new window), ROOST’s self-hosted review console Coop⁠(opens in a new window), and dedicated CSAM detection services such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window).

It has been revealed that our commitment to collaboration and supporting the broader developer ecosystem also is reflected in our work with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission new guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems. Recently published by the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), this guidance provides developers with practical recommendations for addressing these sensitive situations.

We’ve already seen this guidance lead to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC.

Industry observers note that protecting children also means supporting the specialist child safety investigators working to find victims and stop abuse. As we’ve discussed publicly with Thorn⁠(opens in a latest window), AI can help investigators organize and prioritize information and reduce unnecessary exposure to abusive material.

Recent findings suggest that we’re also supporting child-safety law enforcement units with upcoming tools and trainings on how to use AI in their investigations, including dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. At launch, the first tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material.

The initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. It will introduce the tools and how they fit into investigative work. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences.

In a recent development, these efforts share one goal: preventing harm to children and strengthening the response when abuse occurs. We’ll continue improving our safeguards while empowering child protection organizations, developers, researchers, and investigators with the tools, resources, and expertise they need to protect children, combat exploitation, and bring perpetrators to justice. By working together, we can harness the power of AI to make a meaningful difference in the fight against child sexual exploitation and abuse.

#26642. Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (211 w)

Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27057v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.

Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced Hierarchy-Aware Semi-Supervised Graph Classification

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (157 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27043v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semi-supervised graph classification aims to learn graph-level representations by leveraging a large number of unlabeled graphs alongside a small set of labeled ones, effectively mitigating the issue of label scarcity. Despite significant progress by various semi-supervised learning strategies, complex relationships among graph vertices beyond pairwise edges, especially hierarchical structures, remain underexplored by existing methods. In this work, we propose a Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced hierarchy-aware framework, namely HypSEE, for semi-supervised graph classification. Specifically, we first construct walk-induced and embedding-derived hypergraphs to capture hierarchy-aware local and long-range higher-order relationships within graphs. Then, we devise a hierarchical hypergraph pooling approach guided by hypergraph structural entropy (HSE) to facilitate hierarchical representation learning in hypergraphs. Lastly, we employ an anchor graph-based consistency strategy to mutually align the representations from these two hypergraph views, enhancing the learning efficacy on unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on 8 benchmark datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our approach.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Builder Relations and AI Frameworks, MongoDB.

Co-authors:Ajay Tandon, MongoDBNasit Qureshi, MongoDB.

It has been revealed that the MongoDB Integration for Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) helps you build agents that can store sessions and long-term memory with MongoDB. As agents move into production, they need more than powerful models. They need secure, dependable access to data and the ability to retain context over time. That means that you need tooling for a data store that provides durable agent memory for agent state. With the MongoDB Google ADK Integration, you can bring retrieval, session persistence, and memory into your agent architecture with a cohesive, ADK-native developer experience.

In a recent development, google's ADK is an open source agent development framework that lets you build, debug, and deploy reliable AI agents at enterprise scale. It's available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin.

Google ADK offers you an extensive set of tools so you can create, deploy, assess, and scale agents, and it lets you build anything from personal AI assistants to mission-critical business workflows.

You can prototype an agent that searches a product catalog or knowledge base, then evolve it into a production experience that preserves user context across conversations and recalls relevant prior interactions. With MongoDB as a unified data layer, you can store search data, vital conversation states, and agent memories directly alongside your application data. When you use MongoDB, there's no separate database to set up for retrieval, no pipeline syncing application data into a different memory index, and no added latency pulling context from another system before the agent can respond.

Recent findings suggest that ADK supplies the agent framework and tool interface: this integration provides the data and persistence layer beneath it, so you can easily take an agent from prototype to production. These agents can maintain conversation and session memory independent of any single machine, and they can carry a user's history across sessions.

Sources indicate that at the core of this integration is Google ADK 2.0, which serves as the code-first orchestration layer for multi-agent systems. ADK 2.0 provides the deployment framework, while MongoDB provides session and memory storage for agents.

According to recent reports, integrating directly with Gemini platform, ADK 2.0 eliminates the need for custom routing logic by providing standardized tool-calling interfaces, native telemetry, and enterprise access controls by default. You can use Gemini 4 Argon for multi-step reasoning and Gemini 3.8 Flash for low-latency execution.

Great agent experiences improve with context. This integration introduces the MongoDbSessionService class to persist sessions, events, and application-, user-, and session-scoped state to MongoDB.

It has been revealed that this persistence means that you can build agents that retain the context that they need for longer-running and multi-turn interactions. The session service includes optimistic concurrency control to help applications safely manage concurrent updates, while configurable collections make it easier to fit the service into existing data architectures.

For agents that need memory beyond a single session, the MongoDbMemoryService class ingests session events into MongoDB collections and it recalls relevant memories through keyword matching. Memory ingestion is idempotent, which prevents duplicates when the application adds a session again. The following sample shows how you can add the MongoDbMemoryService class to your agent:.

Together, these services help agents become more useful over time without requiring you to connect separate systems for retrieval, state, and memory.

Sources indicate that having memory for agent state is essential, but agents also need fast access to the operational data that they search over—the same product catalogs, documents, and records that your application already queries. You can also add MongoDB Search capability to your agents with ADK integration. This feature gives agents access to the right information and context at the right time, so they can deliver better responses in production. Whether you're building product discovery, knowledge assistants, support experiences, or domain-specific copilots, agents can automatically use semantic and hybrid retrieval to ground their responses in your data.

The following Python code reveals how to add that capability:.

According to recent reports, the application owns the database connection, database name, and search configuration. The agent gets focused tools to call, without exposing those operational details in its context.

Sources indicate that when you use MongoDB as the operational data store, the memory layer for agent state, and the search engine over both, you get one platform instead of three, on whatever deployment you run it on. There's no separate vector database to set up, no search engine to sync against a second copy of the data, and no added latency from the agent switching between systems before it can respond.

According to recent reports, the integration supports MongoDB Atlas and self-managed MongoDB 8.0+ deployments for vector and hybrid search. You can provide a connection string or bring an existing PyMongo client, and configure the following search settings through the MongoDbToolSettings class, including index names, embedding fields, limits, and candidate counts.

That flexibility makes it possible to align the integration with existing data models, deployment choices, and performance requirements.

Industry News: Ruby: State-of-the-Art Potency Prediction across Discovery Regimes Using Learned Structural Representations

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.27015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small-molecule drug discovery proceeds through repeated design-make-test-analyze cycles. The goal is often to maximize potency while keeping other properties within the ranges required for a viable therapeutic candidate. Compound prioritization places different demands on computational methods as drug discovery progresses from hit identification through hit-to-lead and lead optimization, with changing computational budgets and increasing amounts of on-target experimental data. We introduce Ruby, a Robust Universal Binding affinitY predictor that uses intermediate representations from the structural foundation model Pearl without requiring an explicit binding pose for every compound. Ruby is trained on proprietary data plus GenesisPotency-2026, an audited public-source potency training dataset released for academic and commercial use under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license with row-level provenance and audit annotations. Ruby achieves the highest aggregate early enrichment across seven public hit-identification targets among evaluated methods, with adjustable inference effort trading off enrichment and computational cost over more than two orders of magnitude. Ruby achieves the highest average correlations across four public benchmarks: OpenFE, CASP16, FEP+ 4, and OpenBind. Ruby significantly outperforms other methods in zero-shot prediction across eight biochemical and cellular assays from five ongoing Genesis-Incyte programs, widening its performance advantage relative to the public benchmarks. Ruby continues to improve more than other methods when all are given the opportunity to recalibrate using earlier assay measurements. Together, these contributions provide an annotated training resource for the field and a state-of-the-art potency predictor for broad screening, prioritization within related chemical series, and assay-specific prediction as experimental measurements accumulate.

FoRe: A Force-Guided Framework for Autonomous Grasp Recovery in Vision-Language-Action Models

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (219 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in grasp-based manipulation, yet reliable recovery from local grasping failures remains challenging. Specifically, in pick-and-place tasks, policies may continue transport after a failed grasp instead of retrying, potentially reflecting overreliance on proprioceptive cues for stage progression and limited retry supervision. Existing recovery approaches typically rely on deployment-time guidance or demonstration augmentation. We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures. Using force feedback, FoRe partitions demonstrations into approach-grasp and transport-placement stages to train separate policies. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach-grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. We also construct LIBERO-SUCTION, a force-augmented suction manipulation benchmark adapted from LIBERO, with complete demonstration trajectories for policy training. FoRe consistently improves task success rates for VLA-Adapter and $\pi_{0.5}$ on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-SUCTION, average absolute gains are 18.4% and 6.5%, respectively. The corresponding real-world absolute gains are 25.0% and 21.7%. FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.26999v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. Second, the language decision model (e.g., \jev{}) reads these indicators together with the customer's profile and activity, judges the case in context with broad world knowledge, and returns the score of high risk. We evaluate JevRisk on the anti-money laundering task with public synthetic data from Scotiabank and on the credit risk task with real data from Home Credit and Lending Club. On both tasks, JevRisk outperforms rule-based and unsupervised methods, and is on par with or better than supervised methods (e.g., GBDT and TabPFN) trained on about a thousand labelled customers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.
  • According to recent reports, the program began as a pilot in July.
  • Recent findings suggest that participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 16, 2026 · Research · Science.

We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, the program began as a pilot in July. Applications for the next round open Monday, November 23. We’ll award 50,000 newly introduced grants to eligible researchers on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant gives the recipient and up to two collaborators free access to ChatGPT Plus. If you’re already on the waitlist and qualify, we’ll email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

Recent findings suggest that participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research. By default, we don’t use data shared through the program to train our models.

Waitlist signups by country or territory as of November 12, 2026. Darker colors indicate more signups on a logarithmic scale.

20,000 researchers in 33 countries have joined the program since the pilot began in July. Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, looks for upcoming drug targets that could ultimately shorten tuberculosis treatment. He is exploring whether ChatGPT can help link lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development. Arthur Porto, assistant curator of AI biodiversity at the Florida Museum of Natural History, and his team uses AI tools to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases. They also created a 3D model of a butterfly whose wings change color as you turn it, just like the real specimen.

We’re also publishing Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, new research from our Economic Research team examining how more than 1,800 researchers used ChatGPT during the program’s summer pilot. Surveyed participants estimated that, without AI, the same research work at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

We want more researchers to have the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions and make discoveries that improve people’s lives. That is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

It has been revealed that the program’s summer pilot helped us understand how researchers use ChatGPT and how we can improve their experience. Based on feedback from researchers, we’re moving away from lottery-based selection. For the next round, we’ll provide access to the first 50,000 applications who meet the eligibility requirements.

Sources indicate that the pilot gave researchers access to ChatGPT Pro. When we reviewed pilot usage, we found that most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus usage limits. Based on that finding, we’re offering Plus for new grants so we can extend access to more research teams.

Each grant for this round covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers. Our goal for the program as a whole is to reach 200,000 researchers, double the goal we announced when the pilot introduced in July.

It has been revealed that we’ll continue learning from participants about the application process, the capabilities they need, and the support that helps them use these tools in their research. This feedback will help us refine the program and shape future rounds.

It has been revealed that different scientific fields will use AI in different ways, and researchers will need different kinds and levels of support. We’re working with scientific communities to understand those needs and shape our tools, training, and programs around them.

Our support also includes helping scientific communities turn AI-generated results into deeper understanding and fresh discoveries. In mathematics, we contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative⁠ to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

We’re also providing different ways for researchers and institutions to access our tools. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one way we’re helping researchers access advanced AI tools.

Through ChatGPT Edu⁠(opens in a fresh window), universities can give their campus communities access to ChatGPT for research, teaching, and learning, with tools for analyzing data and administrative controls for managing access.

In a recent development, for researchers working in biology, GPT‑Rosalind⁠ brings together specialized biological reasoning and access to scientific tools and databases. The Rosalind Academic Proposal⁠ helps bring these capabilities to eligible labs at U.S. universities, offering up to 30 seats at no cost for up to 12 months. Access to GPT‑Rosalind requires approval through our trusted-access process.

Visit our researcher access guide to learn more about ChatGPT Edu, GPT‑Rosalind, and ChatGPT for Academic Researchers.

In a recent development, as these efforts grow, researchers’ experiences will help us understand where our tools are useful, where they fall short, and what support is needed. We’ll use that feedback to improve our programs, develop training and learning resources, and create opportunities for researchers to exchange approaches with one another.

Our goal is to give more researchers the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions—and to keep improving that support as their research and our capabilities evolve.

Learn more about the program⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (257 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.26980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.

#26626. ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3605 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stop attacks, reduce risk, and advance your security.
  • Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram.
  • According to recent reports, on Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stop attacks, reduce risk, and advance your security.

Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram.

According to recent reports, on Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05. We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local. Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability.

ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account.

ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant upcoming insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat.

Moving laterally from the Remote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft.

Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of events.

Recent findings suggest that following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as /sdk and /ui. The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of ARMORY CASTLE’s remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW.

Figure 2: ARMORY CASTLE nmap port scanning.

ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to internal Linux appliances within the environment that lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. ARMORY CASTLE deployed five newly identified malware families and utilities: the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, the BONESAW remote exploitation utility, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility. ARMORY CASTLE also deployed the LAZYBONES backdoor, which Mandiant and GTIG previously observed in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion.

To establish a foothold on the first Linux appliance, the actor dropped a webshell ActiveSer.jsp, tracked by Mandiant as SLIMSAVAGE. SLIMSAVAGE functions as an upgraded command execution webshell that utilizes the authentication secret pwd=123.

Recent findings suggest that by leveraging ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", ...), the SLIMSAVAGE webshell executed commands inside a command line interpreter, enabled shell pipelines, redirects, creation of environment variables, and chained execution. The webshell reads from both standard output (getInputStream()) and standard error (getErrorStream()), ensuring full diagnostic visibility. It also calls Process.waitFor() and appends the final process return code (\nEXIT:).

According to recent reports, roughly 4 hours later, ARMORY CASTLE deployed an additional webshell to the Linux appliance, u.jsp, tracked as CAGEMATCH. While SLIMSAVAGE provided the group with a robust capability to execute commands on the appliance, the group was limited in their ability to transfer data. To solve this challenge, CAGEMATCH acts as a dedicated payload staging webshell. The webshell checks for a multipart/form-data request header, parses the boundary delimiter, and extracts raw file bytes along with the original filename.

Figure 4: CAGEMATCH File Staging Logic.

CAGEMATCH creates the /tmp directory if necessary, saves the uploaded payload directly to /tmp/, and echoes the absolute target path back to the client. When accessed without an upload payload, it returns a minimal HTML upload form. This provides the attacker with a streamlined post-exploitation workflow: using CAGEMATCH to upload binary payloads, scripts, or tools from the Remote Support appliance directly into /tmp, and subsequently invoke SLIMSAVAGE to adjust execution permissions and execute the staged tools.

To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary /bin/env. ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary /bin/env, any user would be allowed to execute commands as root.

Figure 5: ARMORY CASTLE gdb Privilege Escalation.

After successfully escalating privileges to root, ARMORY CASTLE began staging additional tooling on the Linux appliance to enable lateral movement within the environment. ARMORY CASTLE used curl to download the RAR utility from the Remote Support appliance.

Figure 6: ARMORY CASTLE downloads staged RAR utility.

ARMORY CASTLE then utilized curl to download a rar archive 123.rar which was subsequently extracted using their downloaded RAR binary.

Figure 7: ARMORY CASTLE extracts BONESAW.

Tracked as BONESAW, /tmp/123 is a remote exploitation utility written in Golang that leverages CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter to enable remote arbitrary LMDB exfiltration, SAML STS hijacking, and SSO administrator account creation. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leveraging this utility to target an internal vCenter server, successfully creating an SSO admin account, exfiltrating and parsing the LMDB which enabled lateral movement to the server.

BONESAW achieves full system compromise against vCenter Server 7.x and 8.x appliances through the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. This vulnerability exploits a cryptographic logic and authorization flaw in VMware's rpc_srp_verifier service over port 2012, exposing a shared session key that can be used to create authenticated sessions as administrator@vsphere.local. BONESAW also provides the ability to stream the raw underlying LMDB file for offline parsing, extract the VMware Security Token Service (STS) SAML private RSA signing key, create a backdoor machine account via vmdir, forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertion tokens, and assign Global Administrator privileges on the vCenter root folder via the vSphere SOAP API.

According to recent reports, while CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309, primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password, there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server vmdir daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the vmdir DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords.

In a recent development, mandiant has evidence that ARMORY CASTLE had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026. Logs indicate that BONESAW was executed in early September 2026 against a vCenter server already patched against CVE-2026-59309, and the recovered Go binary contains a build timestamp of 2026-07-13T09:21:24Z (16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed), although Go build metadata can be modified prior to compilation.

ARMORY CASTLE named BONESAW vcenter-db-teamcheck-go and compiled it in a Windows development environment based on Golang build artifacts: E:/CodeFiles/VulnScan/Vcenter/go_teamcheck/. BONESAW supports multiple command-line arguments, with primary functionality centered on the csa subcommand to remotely create an SSO admin account.

Figure 8: BONESAW Command Line Arguments.

When executed utilizing the CSA command line flag, BONESAW creates the following files on disk:.

Figure 9: BONESAW Filesystem Artifacts.

SAWSNAKE parses command-line arguments to determine its operating mode and supports the following command line arguments:.

Figure 10: SAWSNAKE Command Line Arguments.

SAWSNAKE creates the following files on disk:.

Figure 11: Files created by SAWSNAKE.

It has been revealed that mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Consistent with earlier activity, ARMORY CASTLE deleted SAWSNAKE and its output files from disk using rm.

Shortly after the deployment of SAWSNAKE, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged an additional backdoor /tmp/dbr tracked as BEARBONES. BEARBONES is written in C and is based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server. It is capable of bypassing system password authentication when using password-based authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from /tmp instead of the default directory /etc/dropbear. The authentication handler svr_auth_password for the packet type SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST was backdoored to bypass /etc/shadow validation and grant access if the SHA-256 digest of the first 14 bytes of client password matches a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, while also logging plaintext credentials. Additionally, the internal version string and the session identification string were modified to “23345” and “SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345”. Pivoting on this SSH banner identified a suspected obfuscation network of compromised third-party firewalls and routers exposing SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 on non-standard high TCP ports.

ARMORY CASTLE executed BEARBONES several times from the Linux appliance, first attempting to open a listener on TCP port 53 and later on TCP port 33992.

Figure 12: BEARBONES Command Line Execution.

After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-@vsphere.local. Notably, ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. Mandiant also observed this TTP during BRICKSTORM intrusions conducted by suspected PRC-nexus actor UNC6201. After enabling SSH, ARMORY CASTLE connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account.

ARMORY CASTLE then conducted credential theft, targeting the vCenter internal master crypto key file as well as the PostgreSQL password file using SSH. ARMORY CASTLE disabled the SSH service via the VAMI API immediately after extracting the vCenter master symmetric key and PostgreSQL database credentials. ARMORY CASTLE then was observed authenticating to ESXi Host Client (“ESXUI”) using the vpxuser account and also connected to it via SSH using the root account.

Recent findings suggest that ARMORY CASTLE used the WinSCP client to enumerate the ESXi file system, attached disks, mounted Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys. ARMORY CASTLE conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account. The actor was primarily observed enumerating directories and VMFS volumes. To stage and exfiltrate data from the ESXi filesystem, ARMORY CASTLE created a hidden directory, .a, on a VMFS volume to which they established an SCP connection to the ESXi using scp -r -d -t "/vmfs/volumes//.a". ARMORY CASTLE then staged and extracted a suspected VMware specific toolset onto the ESXi host using tar xzf vmfs-pydist.tar.gz.

Figure 13: ARMORY CASTLE reconnaissance of guest VMs.

ARMORY CASTLE then archived the extracted files into o.tar.gz, copied the archive from the ESXi filesystem using scp -r -p -d -f "o.tar.gz", and deleted the hidden .a directory. On the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE staged the corresponding OpenSSH RSA private key at /tmp/123.key (matching the public key added to ESXi root authorized_keys) to authenticate outbound from the Linux appliance to ESXi over SSH without a password, alongside the BEARBONES SSH listener on the Linux appliance. From the Linux appliance, staged archives were downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance, from which ARMORY CASTLE likely exfiltrated the data.

Figure 14: ARMORY CASTLE SSH Tunnel.

ARMORY CASTLE deployed a Slack-based backdoor tracked as LAZYBONES (/usr/bin/vmtoolscs) to an additional Linux appliance alongside the /tmp/123.key SSH private key. ARMORY CASTLE established persistence using a systemd service file set to restart every 50 minutes. LAZYBONES is a lightweight backdoor, written in Go, that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication over HTTPS using Slack. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Specifically, this variant encrypts Slack C2 messages with AES-256-CTR prior to Base64 encoding, polls with a 150 to 450 second jitter interval, and supports four commands (cmd, upload, download, and sleep) for command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE deploying LAZYBONES in a separate campaign in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of CVE-2025-22457.

According to recent reports, GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog, the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity.

It has been revealed that while GTIG and Mandiant have tracked ARMORY CASTLE exploiting zero-days and n-days in edge and security appliances for initial access since 2023, BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days. The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each. The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations. It also demonstrates the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets. Lastly, it is key to highlight that the build time of BONESAW predates its deployment in this intrusion by over a month, indicating it was likely developed for broader operations.

The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by ARMORY CASTLE underscores a reality: virtualization infrastructure such as VMware vCenter remains a prime target for advanced persistent threats (APTs). Because vCenter serves as the centralized control plane for the virtualized data center, relying solely on reactive patching is insufficient to protect it. Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities.

Sources indicate that for a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide  vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide. This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor.

To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch.

The Risks of Default Configurations: The VCSA Host-Based Firewall.

A common misconception in defending the vCenter control plane is that the native VCSA host-based firewall managed via the Virtual Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) provides adequate protection against lateral movement. In practice, relying on this default GUI-based firewall introduces severe operational and security limitations that threat actors like ARMORY CASTLE exploit:.

Industry observers note that lack of Port-Specific Granularity: The native VAMI GUI lacks the precision required for a Zero Trust model. To grant an internal server (such as a backup server) legitimate access to the vSphere API on TCP 443, an administrator is often forced to trust that IP for all ports. If that internal server is compromised, the attacker inherits an unobstructed path to highly sensitive management interfaces like SSH (22) and the VAMI (5480).

Sources indicate that circular Administrative Dependency: The VCSA firewall is managed via the VAMI, which resides on TCP port 5480. If an attacker gains VAMI access as ARMORY CASTLE demonstrated to enable SSH,  they can use their compromised role to deactivate the firewall entirely.

Forensic Visibility Gaps: The VAMI firewall is designed for connectivity management, not security monitoring, and does not generate remote logs for denied connection attempts or shell activity. This blinds the SOC to active lateral movement and port scanning.

In a recent development, inbound-Only Policy: The default GUI focuses exclusively on inbound traffic, leaving outbound (egress) policy unmanaged. This allows malware on a compromised VCSA to communicate freely with external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure.

Proactive Hardening with the VCSA Hardening Tool.

To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool.

Sources indicate that this script bypasses the vulnerable VAMI GUI and enforces security configurations directly at the Photon Linux kernel level via iptables. By transitioning the appliance to a strict "Default Deny" posture, enforcing granular egress filtering, and bridging kernel-level events to a remote SIEM, the tool transforms the VCSA from a passive appliance into an active security sensor.

The table below illustrates how deploying this proactive hardening script would have disrupted ARMORY CASTLE's attack chain at multiple stages, demonstrating its efficacy against zero-day exploits.

Impact on the ARMORY CASTLE Attack Chain.

Protection Against Future Zero-Days.

VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy & Connection Logging (Management Ports).

Sources indicate that the nmap scans targeting TCP ports 443, 5480, and 22 are silently dropped because the attacker's source IP is not in the trusted whitelists. These blocked connection attempts are instantly forwarded to the SIEM via the iptables-log-bridge.sh service, exposing the active network reconnaissance.

Conceals critical management interfaces from internal network mapping tools and provides high-fidelity, early-warning alerts of active lateral movement before exploitation can occur.

VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 443).

Provides defense-in-depth: Even if a zero-day allows credential theft or authentication bypass on a backend service, the stolen credentials/tokens cannot be used to access the management plane from an untrusted network.

VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 2010).

An iptables DROP policy on TCP 2012 for non-allowlisted IPs prevents the exploit payload originating from a compromised Linux appliance from reaching the vmdird service.

Drops unauthorized inbound connections to management interfaces and RPC services, mitigating network-level exploitation of vulnerable services.

VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 22 & 5480).

In a recent development, blocks the OS-level pivot. The firewall drops the PUT request to the VAMI API (TCP 5480 or 443) used to enable the SSH daemon. Furthermore, even if SSH was already enabled, the VCSA_SSH_RULES chain drops all SSH connections.

Protects the underlying OS and databases from direct credential theft or tampering. Even if an attacker gains administrative privileges within the web application, they are blocked from dropping down to a root shell.

VCSA iptables Egress DROP Policy.

An egress DROP policy prevents SCP data exfiltration and blocks the LAZYBONES backdoor from establishing HTTPS C2 communications with external Slack endpoints.

Blocks unauthorized outbound internet and internal network connections, preventing the VCSA from acting as a pivot point or establishing external C2.

VCSA OS-Level Command and Syslog Auditing.

Remote syslog forwarding captures the execution of tar and Python vmfs_browser.py over SSH, exposing the extraction of NTDS.dit and registry hives in real-time.

Forwards bash command execution and dropped network packets to a SIEM, bypassing local anti-forensics (e.g., .bash_history deletion) and alerting on unauthorized shell activity.

VCSA Kernel-Level Rule Enforcement.

iptables rules operate independently of the VAMI application, preventing the actor from using the VAMI API (/rest/appliance/access/ssh) to circumvent network security controls.

Decouples network security from the vCenter application layer, ensuring firewall policies cannot be modified via compromised VAMI or vSphere administrative credentials.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we’re launching OpenAI for Chile, a partnership with the Government of Chile, led by the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, to support responsible AI adoption in public administration, build civil servants’ skills and help local startups develop useful AI applications.

The partnership builds on Chile’s National AI Policy and action initiative⁠(opens in a new window), which support talent development, research and responsible adoption.

The Memorandum of Understanding was signed on the sidelines of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in California, with Minister Ximena Lincolao leading the agreement on behalf of Chile.

According to recent reports, the partnership is supported by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s American SI Exports Program⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), of which OpenAI is an anchor partner, helping Chile advance its own AI ambitions through public sector innovation, skills development, and entrepreneurship.

The partnership will explore technology adoption in the ministry’s administrative processes, including potential support from OpenAI on adopting fresh models, alongside advice and training for ministry personnel.

For civil servants, the partnership will explore practical AI literacy, upskilling and reskilling tailored to their roles. Activities could include workshops and a train-the-trainer approach, covering effective use of AI tools, checking outputs, protecting sensitive information and maintaining human oversight.

To support Chile’s AI startup and innovation ecosystem, the partners will explore access to relevant OpenAI programs and technology, practical learning, technical guidance and mentorship. Cooperation could also connect entrepreneurs with public institutions, universities and other local partners to develop applications that support Chile’s economic development and public-service priorities.

A joint task force of ministry and OpenAI representatives is expected to agree priorities and an initial workplan, with leads, milestones and measures of success for each activity.

Sources indicate that specific activities, eligibility, resources and access to technology will be agreed separately. The MoU sets no investment or purchasing commitment. Activities will be subject to appropriate safeguards for privacy, information security and responsible use.

According to recent reports, openAI for Chile is part of OpenAI for Countries, our global initiative to help countries use AI to advance their national priorities, strengthen their economies and expand opportunity. We work with governments and local partners to turn AI’s potential into practical benefits for their people.

When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (168 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.26972v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.

Beyond Prompt Heuristics: Assessing Child Safety Alignment in LLMs

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (157 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.26965v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.

Director, State, Local, Higher Ed Central, Google Public Sector.

As state and local agencies modernize to meet evolving public needs, leaders have an unprecedented opportunity to empower and elevate their teams. Modernizing public sector operations starts with giving dedicated public servants the right tools to thrive. By replacing repetitive administrative routines with intuitive, intelligent workflows, agencies can free their staff to do what they do best: focus on high-impact problem-solving, build rewarding careers, and deliver responsive, compassionate services to the residents and communities they serve.

It has been revealed that modernizing an agency workforce means transitioning employees from institutional systems to agentic platforms—redirecting their efforts away from manual administration and freeing up time for high-touch service delivery. By leveraging Google Cloud’s integrated stack to modernize daily operations, agency leaders can reliably meet regulatory requirements while creating the operational capacity to innovate, develop staff, and strengthen public trust.

According to recent reports, under the leadership of CIO Ted Ross, the City of Los Angeles addressed administrative constraints by deploying Google Workspace with Gemini across its entire 27,500-person municipal workforce. City employees now use agents to instantly synthesize large amounts of grant documents buried in silos and quickly rewrite public web copy for clearer readability. This digital companion allows city staff to step away from time-consuming administrative tasks and spend more time focusing on critical community service delivery, ensuring the city is operationally ready to host major global events like the 2028 Olympics and 2028 Paralympics.

The University of Hawaii needed a better way to keep local talent from leaving the islands. To build and retain regional talent, the university turned to BigQuery and Gemini—creating an automated, skills-first platform that helps match individuals with career opportunities. This solution maps student and faculty capabilities, matches individuals to academic roles and public research projects, and helps retain top talent.

The Indiana Department of Transportation was issued an urgent executive mandate requiring a comprehensive review of complex legal contracts within a strict 30-day window. The agency deployed Gemini to securely ingest, parse, and analyze the state’s contract repositories. The automated system successfully isolated key legal parameters, saving 360 hours of highly skilled engineering labor and meeting the strict deadline.

In a recent development, A similar transformation occurred within Maryland’s state agencies, where caseworkers navigating complex public benefits documentation spent hours indexing files and searching manual handbooks to find specific clause requirements. Maryland deployed Gemini and Gemini Notebook across its 40,000-person state workforce, establishing a secure framework to index and interact with state benefits compliance manuals. Caseworkers can now run plain-language queries to retrieve policy directives in seconds, drastically reducing the administrative processing times for residents.

In a recent development, giving the public sector workforce a secure starting point for enterprise workflows streamlines routine processes, creating the space for employees to expand their skills and lead strategic mission priorities. CENTRY: A Probabilistic Latent-State Model for Continual AI Risk Estimation, Monitoring, and Regulation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (239 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.26940v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. A structured latent-variable model is developed in which the latent representation is decomposed into a fast interaction subspace that captures the evolving AI--environment dynamics and three slow latent subspaces that encode the long-term risk states associated with the dataset, hardware, and model components. Rather than requiring a ground-truth risk label at every time step, the component-risk states are treated as latent variables and are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally informed during training and continual refinement by evidence-supported behavior--cause records. The resulting framework unifies continual probabilistic inference, online risk estimation, and adaptive risk regulation in an implementable architecture. Under the explicit assumptions stated for the corresponding results, we establish formal guarantees spanning safety, learning, inference, and operations, including finite-horizon and asymptotic risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, consistency and identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay, false-alarm, containment, and computational-complexity characterizations.

arXiv:2611.26938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. This paper equips the corrections that act along the direction of movement -- a mean shift, an elongation of the covariance along the path and a skewness -- with the rule they lack: a calibrated gate, driven by a maturity statistic of the population, decides whether, how strongly and for how long each correction acts, and when the gate is closed the algorithm is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (EMNA). The statistic is a cumulative path of whitened mean shifts with an inverse-Wishart correction, whose expectation is one under a null model without systematic movement and whose quantiles give thresholds with known false-alarm rate. It gates the three corrections as three rank-one terms of one matrix sampling equation, the skewness being carried by a skew-normal sampler that preserves the estimated mean and covariance; all vanish at maturity. We call the resulting algorithm the maturity-gated EDA (MG-EDA). A full factorial study on a training set of black-box optimization benchmarking (BBOB) functions separates the parameters: variance scaling is the prerequisite, the mean shift needs a feedback correction removing the injected shift from the statistic, the elongation turns the variance loss on a slope into a gain, and the skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances MG-EDA with the first- and second-order corrections is significantly better than the skewness-only predecessor and than EMNA with variance scaling, ties with EMNA with anticipated mean shift, and trails the adapted maximum-likelihood Gaussian model (AMaLGaM) in 20 dimensions.

Our latest model configuration earned leading marks on multiple benchmarks. Every ChatGPT Enterprise customer can now request access.

Today, we're releasing an updated Astra for Law that is state-of-the-art on Harvey LAB-AA and a top performer on Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench. We are also enabling all ChatGPT Enterprise customers to request access through the Trusted Access Program, including through the API.

Sources indicate that astra for Law is a model configuration of GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠, our latest, most powerful frontier model. It pairs GPT‑6.2 Astra with an expanded legal search index and instructions for researching a question, weighing the authorities, and writing the answer. Today’s configuration earned full credit on the LAB-AA tests nearly 40% more often than did the runner-up, GPT‑6.2 Astra.

Since we introduced Astra for Law in September⁠ to a small group of firms, including Cooley⁠, Ropes & Gray⁠, and Sullivan & Cromwell⁠, our research team has made rapid innovations to improve its legal reasoning and expand its legal search index by over a third. On Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a new window), the share of research answers that passed every check rose from about 46% to 53.8% in less than two months.

In a recent development, as the world grows more complex, lawyers occupy an increasingly vital role. They shape nearly every system we rely on: they negotiate the agreements that move commerce, defend people’s rights in courts, and draft the laws we all live by. That’s why we’ve made law a research priority at OpenAI: to put the best intelligence in the hands of the best lawyers.

It has been revealed that harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) tests whether a model can take a legal assignment from start to finish. LAB-AA⁠(opens in a latest window) is Artificial Analysis’s version of that test. It tests the models on 120 assignments developed by Harvey across 24 areas of law – everything from drafting deposition outlines to reviewing commercial leases to strategizing ownership changes in acquisitions. To earn full credit, an answer must meet every requirement of an assignment without hallucinating, i.e., making a material claim that is not supported by the source documents.

Astra for Law ranked first, earning full credit on 20.8% of assignments, ahead of GPT‑6.2 Astra at 15.0% and Muse Wonder Full at 13.1%.

For legal teams paying by usage, this can mean the difference between staying within budget and blowing through it.

Recent findings suggest that we've made law a research priority at OpenAI, dedicating a team of researchers to accelerate innovation for frontier legal intelligence. Building Astra for Law as a model configuration lets us stay on the bleeding edge of the frontier, in this case GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠. On top of this foundation, we iteratively refine Astra for Law’s specific settings and instructions in response to practitioner feedback, teaching it how to reason and write like a seasoned lawyer. We also continuously hone its tools, such as the legal search index. Since September, we’ve grown the index by 34%, adding over 80 million new URLs, including across international jurisdictions such as the UK, Australia, and Canada. Across law firm customers and OpenAI’s own legal team, early customers are building references around their practice, inviting tougher challenges to their arguments, and finding upcoming ways to respond to changing legislation.

Industry observers note that give your argument its strongest opponent. A common use for Astra for Law is as a sparring partner. A competition lawyer gives it a reading of a statute and asks it to argue the other side, drawing on legislative history, court decisions, and versions of the law in other languages.

It has been revealed that find the line between a recommendation and a requirement. A policy lawyer looking at a proposed oversight bill wanted to know how much power an independent reviewer would have. If the reviewer called for a fix, would the developer have to make it? For questions like these, the lawyer puts a plain-English account of each obligation beside the bill’s exact words, so she can make fast judgment calls about which reading the text supports.

Start the first call with outside counsel on the hardest question. When the business is considering entering an unfamiliar industry, a product lawyer uses Astra for Law to map which rules would apply to the proposed activity. Instead of spending the first call asking for high-level advice, the lawyer can bring outside counsel what’s actually at issue.

Turn a stack of policies into a workflow. A legal program manager used Astra for Law to turn regulatory procedures and company policy into a workflow for colleagues handling incoming cases, enabling them to automate when to ask for more information, when to close the case, and when to escalate it to a lawyer.

Recent findings suggest that build the guide you wish came with the statute. A competition lawyer paired Astra for Law with ChatGPT’s site-building tools to annotate legislation the team uses regularly. A colleague reading a provision can hover over a term for its definition, follow a link to the materials that explain it, and see what the team advised the last time that provision came up.

Starting today, every ChatGPT Enterprise customer can request Astra for Law through the Trusted Access Program in the admin console. If your team already has access, select gpt-6.2-astra-law in ChatGPT. Customers can also request API access to build Astra for Law into their own tools using this form⁠.

It has been revealed that the legal profession is at an inflection point. As technology changes what businesses can do and the world becomes increasingly complex and interconnected, lawyers have an unprecedented opportunity to shape how we make sense of the moment, not just for the businesses they advise but for all of us who live by the rules they help write.

We believe the best lawyers, equipped with the best intelligence, can meet that moment. We’re only at the beginning. We can’t wait to see where you take the profession.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.26936v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against VLMs while preserving visual fidelity. LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence that reveals private information and adapt an invisible perturbation to the target VLM's answers and to an appearance reviewer agent, which rejects any candidate with visible artifacts. We instantiate SecretAgent with two complementary variants: SecretAgent-Gradient optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for cross-model transferability, and the gradient-free SecretAgent-Tool composes procedural noise and achieves the best perceptual fidelity on three of the five datasets. Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.26933v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Analyzing frame similarity and the vision tokenizers of 16 open models, we trace this loss to a step before token selection. Under a token budget, the frames of a long video are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 s over which frames remain similar. The two-frame 3D patches of models such as Qwen-VL then blend two unrelated scenes into each visual token, a double exposure that arises before any pruning or merging. Fixed-size tokenizers such as InternVL's avoid this blend but respond differently to the same reduction. We propose ESSENCE, a training-free method that tokenizes moments, segments within which frames remain similar, rather than frames. Before encoding, a closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and the tokenizer class to set the number of token grids and the dimension to reduce; visual tokens are then released from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5, ESSENCE achieves higher accuracy in 58 of 60 comparisons at matched mean time to first token (TTFT). With 80% of the tokens, it matches the average accuracy of the full Qwen models at $1.6\times$ faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it exceeds the full model by up to 3.4 points. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhkandsrz/ESSENCE.
